english.html: still, when the said Bertrande de Rols had received him for Martin Guerre her husband, from whom afterwards, conversing day and night together, it was easier for him to learn more, and to confirm himself better in what the others had told him — denying always, nevertheless, that he was a Necromancer, or had used any charms, enchantments, or any kind of magic.

Everyone persuaded himself, and with great reason, as I have shown above <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>, that this prodigious imposture was aided by Necromancy, or some other reprobate art: inasmuch as it was impossible by nature to say so many things, and to know persons never before seen, reciting to them the conversations which they and the said Martin Guerre had had ten, fifteen and twenty years before; together with uncovering the most particular and private acts that can pass between two married people, and that had truly taken place between the said Martin Guerre and Bertrande de Rols, husband and wife — without the help of some magic and diabolical art. Whence I cannot yet put off this opinion, though this fine rustic denied it at the execution. Especially when I remember that never did he falter in any interrogation whatever that was put to him by me, or by Monsieur the President, in full chamber, save in this one alone: namely, when the said lord President asked him (as if assured of it) whence he had the familiar spirit of which he had made use in this affair, and where it was that he had learned the diabolical invocations. For then, all affrighted, he lowered his face, and knew not what to answer: making true what Ovid says in some place <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>,

notes.citation: Coras, Annotation LXXI as printed (annot-070 in the transcription, p090–p096), on magic
notes.gloss: The long annotation in which Coras argues that magic is not wholly fabulous and that the laws, divine and human, punish it; his "as I have shown above".

notes.original: Oui. au li. ij. de la metamorphoſe.
notes.gloss: Heu quam difficile est crimen non prodere vultu! — of Callisto, unable to hide her shame before Diana.

english.html: Alas, how hard it is not to betray a crime by the face! (Heu, quàm difficile eſt crimen non prodere vultu!)

lines: cor, quand ladi. Bertrande de Rols l'eut
receu pour Martin Guerre ſon mari, de
laquelle apres en conuerſant iour & nuit
enſemble, luy fut plus aiſé en apprendre
d'auantage, & ſe confermer mieux en ce
que les autres luy auoyẽt dit, niant touſ-
iours toutesfois eſtre Necromantien, &
auoir vſé d'aucuns charmes, enchante-
mens, ou d'aucune eſpece de magie.
Chacun ſe perſuadoit, & à grande raiſon, comme i'ay
deſſus monſtré {a}: que cette prodigieuſe impoſture
eſtoit aidée de Necromantie, ou quelque autre art re-
prouué: d'autant qu'il eſtoit impoſſible par nature, di-
re tant de choſes, & cognoiſtre les perſonnes, non ia-
mais veuës, leur recitant les propos qu'elles, & ledit
Martin Guerre auoyent eu depuis dix, quinze & vingt
ans: enſemble deſçouurir les actes les plus particuliers,
& priuez, qui peuuent eſtre entre deux mariez, & veri-
tablement eſtoyent interuenuz entre leſdicts Martin
Guerre, & Bertande de Rols, mari & femme, ſans le ſe-
cours de quelque magie, & art diabolique. Dont ne
puis-ie encor deſpouiller cette opinion, quoy que ce
gentil ruſtre ait nié en l'execution. Meſmes quand il
me ſouuient, que iamais il ne ſe troubla en interro-
gatoire quelconque qui luy fuſt fait par moy, ou par
Monſieur le Preſident, en plaine chambre, hors-mis en
çeſtuy ſeul: à ſçauoir, quand ledit ſeigneur Preſident luy
demanda (cõme par aſſeurãce) d'où il auoit l'eſprit fa-
milier, duquel il ſ'eſtoit aidé en ce fait, & où eſt-ce qu'il
auoit appriſes les inuocations diaboliques. Car alors
tout effrayé, baiſſa ſon viſage, & ne ſceut que reſpõdre:
rendant veritable, ce que dit Ouide en quelque lieu {b},
Heu, quàm difficile eſt crimen non prodere
vultu!
En l'anno-
tation lxxi.
Oui. au li.
ij. de la meta-
morphoſe.
